summary: The eight interviews do not support the three hypotheses as a set. None of the ten quotes from six participants shows a hypothesis as written. Two of ten techniques, the case matrix and the analysis of competing hypotheses, can reach the strength of statement needed, which was to show a link between things. Both agreed with the other eight, and no change to the inclusion rules reversed the reading.

The hypothesis that customers find voice AI more satisfying than traditional voice automation leans favourable, because three participants speak well of it and a fourth comes round, while two object. No quote compares the voice AI with traditional voice automation, so that hypothesis cannot be tested. The hypothesis that customers do not hang up immediately on learning they are speaking with an AI, and the hypothesis that they do not immediately ask for a human, are each contradicted only by hypothetical statements from two participants. Whether they count as contradicted or untested depends on how the cause of a hang-up is defined. Where leaving or asking for a human is imagined, it happens at the start of the call.

The overall reading, that no hypothesis is shown, deserves more trust than the details. The quotation and spot checks passed, but all techniques read the same quotes and used the same model, so their agreement checks the method and is not independent evidence. The main limit is the material: only six of the eight participants are quoted, the basis for choosing them is not given, and every hang-up and human request is hypothetical, from participants who heard prerecorded scenarios. No person reviewed the results.
The analysis leaves open how common these views are and whether the voice AI itself, apart from the voice, the introduction and earlier experience, drives the reactions.

conclusions.title: The quotes do not show support for the three hypotheses as a set.
conclusions.text: The first hypothesis (voice AI is more satisfying than traditional voice automation) has a favourable direction from three participants but is not tested as a comparison. The second hypothesis (customers do not hang up immediately on learning it is an AI) and the third hypothesis (customers do not immediately ask for a human) receive no affirming statement, and each is contradicted only by the hypothetical statements of two participants. When 21 changes to the inclusion rules were tried, none produced support for the first hypothesis as a comparison, for the second or for the third.
conclusions.label: high
conclusions.reason: All ten techniques agree on the direction. The techniques read the quotes in different ways: the case matrix, hypothesis tree and framework matrix lay the quotes out by participant, the content analysis, stance detection and word-cue count tally them, the thematic analysis reads them for meaning, the competing hypotheses matrix rates them against rival explanations, and the disconfirmation search looked for statements that would overturn the reading and found none. The sensitivity test found no reversal in 21 changed rows. The quotation and spot checks passed.

conclusions.title: No quote compares the voice AI with traditional voice automation, so the first hypothesis as worded is untested.
conclusions.text: The comparators named are website chat bots (P1), a robot voice (P2) and having to repeat yourself (P3). Only P2's remark that a robot "sounds more like a robot voice" refers to a voice system, and it is an indirect comparison. Satisfaction relative to traditional voice automation therefore cannot be read from these quotes.
conclusions.label: high
conclusions.reason: Nine techniques agree, and the disconfirmation search partly agrees: it found that P2's remark is one indirect voice comparison, so the wording here says no direct comparison and not no comparison at all. The techniques read the quotes in different ways (tabulation by participant, word-cue counting, stance labels, a search for disconfirming statements, and a re-run with a stricter rule for the comparator). The checks passed. The stance detection repeat run gave the same label on 28 of 30 targets, and the two differences (P5's car accident quote on the first hypothesis and P5's hang-up quote on the second) do not change which comparators were named.

conclusions.title: Every hang-up and human-request statement is hypothetical, so no behaviour was observed.
conclusions.text: Participants heard prerecorded scenarios, and each relevant statement uses "would" or "if I was". P1's second quote reports that a human could be requested, which describes what the scenario offered. The quotes therefore show intentions, which may overstate or understate what customers do in a live call.
conclusions.label: high
conclusions.reason: All ten techniques agree, using different readings, including a tense check in the disconfirmation search (no observed behaviour found) and a sensitivity row that removes every hypothetical statement. The checks passed.

conclusions.title: Two of the eight participants have no quote, and the basis for choosing the quotes is not given.
conclusions.text: P8 and P9 are not quoted, and the material says only that some participants are quoted. Every finding therefore covers six participants and ten selected quotes. If the selection favoured strong reactions, the split between favourable and unfavourable views would be exaggerated.
conclusions.label: high
conclusions.reason: All ten techniques report the gap, and the sensitivity test bounded it by assuming invented positions for P8 and P9, which could produce at most a tie. This is a finding about what the material contains, and the checks passed.

conclusions.title: Quoted participants are split on the voice AI, with three favourable and three unfavourable at least once.
conclusions.text: P1, P2 and P3 speak well of it, and P4 reaches approval after initial reluctance. P5 and P10 object, and P1 also records annoyance in a second quote. Depending on how P1, P4 and the context-specific complaints are coded, the split is a tie or four favourable against two unfavourable.
conclusions.label: medium
conclusions.reason: Eight techniques agree on the split, using different readings (participant matrix, tree of sub-claims, themes, stance labels, content codes and a rival-hypotheses rating). The word-cue count only partly agrees because its lexicon wrongly counted the word robot in P2's quote as negative. The sensitivity test shows the exact balance changes with the coding. In the stance detection repeat run, the label for P5's car accident quote on the first hypothesis differed on one of two runs, and that quote is one of the unfavourable quotes. The label is medium for these reasons, although the checks passed.
conclusions.caveat: The exact balance between favourable and unfavourable changes depending on how the quotes are coded, and one repeat run labelled one of the unfavourable quotes differently. The split is therefore a tie or four against two, not a fixed count.

conclusions.title: The second hypothesis is untested as worded: no quote links a hang-up to learning that it is an AI.
conclusions.text: P10 says "I would've definitely have hung up at the intro" and gives the reason as "way too long". P5 would probably have hung up only if no human was provided. No quote says a participant would stay on the line, and P4's move from reluctance to approval is at most weak support. The material does not say where the AI is disclosed.
conclusions.label: medium
conclusions.reason: The techniques agree on the facts but differ in the label they give the second hypothesis, and the cause is a difference in definition. Where hanging up counts as evidence against that hypothesis whatever its cause (stance detection, word-cue count, framework matrix and the case matrix), it is contradicted for two participants. Where the cause must be learning it is an AI, or where hypothetical statements are excluded, it is untested (hypothesis tree, thematic analysis, content analysis, and the sensitivity test in three of its changed rows). This conclusion takes the stricter definition because it is the wording of the hypothesis. The stance detection repeat run gave a different label for P5's hang-up quote on one of two runs. One verification finding limits it: the disconfirmation search found that P5's reference to "AI in its current state" means the disclosure cannot be ruled out as a driver.
conclusions.caveat: The techniques disagree on whether the second hypothesis is contradicted or untested, because the answer depends on whether any hang-up counts or only one caused by learning it is an AI. A check also found that the AI itself cannot be ruled out as the reason for P5's hang-up.

conclusions.title: The third hypothesis is not supported, and two participants say they would ask for a human, as hedged intentions.
conclusions.text: P4 says they would probably want to speak to someone "at first" and, about asking at the introduction, "If I was gonna do it, that's probably where I would do it". P5 says "I would've asked for a human." with no timing. No quote says a participant would decline to ask, and the silence of P1, P2 and P3 is not evidence of a view.
conclusions.label: medium
conclusions.reason: Eight techniques agree that the third hypothesis is contradicted for P4 and P5 and that nothing supports it, reading the quotes in different ways (matrix, tree, themes, stance labels, counts and ratings). The disconfirmation search limits the conclusion: P4's statement is hedged twice, the note naming the introduction is the compiler's gloss and not P4's words, and P5 gives no timing, so "immediately" is not confirmed. The sensitivity test shows the contradiction rests on one participant each in several rows and becomes untested when hypothetical statements are excluded. The checks passed.
conclusions.caveat: Support is weaker because P4's statement is hedged, the link to the introduction comes from the compiler's note, and P5 gives no timing. The contradiction also rests on one participant each in several changed rows and disappears when hypothetical statements are excluded.

conclusions.title: Participants tie reservations to the voice, a stressful setting, a long introduction and earlier experience, but not separably from the AI itself.
conclusions.text: P10 objects that the voice is American and "sounds very much like an AI voice", P5 calls the voice "very cold in clinical" and imagines a car accident, P10 calls the introduction too long, and P1 refers to earlier experiences with AI agents. Several techniques read these as context and not as rejection of voice AI. The disconfirmation search points out that P5 also names "AI in its current state", and that the link between P5's car accident quote and the motor claim scenario is inferred, not recorded.
conclusions.label: medium
conclusions.reason: Most techniques agree that reservations point to named features, and they read the quotes in different ways. The conflict is between findings worded as context and not the AI (case matrix, thematic analysis, framework matrix) and the disconfirmation search, which shows that P10's quote about the American AI voice and P5's quote about AI in its current state name the AI, and that one driver does not cover P10's voice quote and P1's annoyance at earlier experiences. The cause is the wording of those quotes combined with the absence of any record of where the AI is disclosed, so the conflict is resolved only by stating several drivers and leaving the AI's own role open, which this conclusion does. A verification finding therefore limits it to medium.
conclusions.caveat: The techniques disagree on whether these reservations are about context or about the AI itself. A check found that two of the quotes name the AI, and the material does not say where the AI is disclosed, so the AI's own role stays open.

conclusions.title: Where leaving or asking for a human is imagined, it is placed at the start of the call.
conclusions.text: P10 places the hang-up "at the intro", and P4's remark about asking for a human is about the introduction. P5 gives no timing, and P4 says the wish to speak to someone changes as the process goes on. The pattern is therefore about the opening moments, and it should not be netted against the favourable reactions, which concern the whole experience.
conclusions.label: medium
conclusions.reason: Three techniques (thematic analysis, framework matrix and content analysis) state the pattern directly, and the others agree in part or list it as an alternative explanation. The wording of the introduction link rests on one explicit quote (P10's hang-up at the intro) and one quote whose timing comes from the compiler's note (P4's remark about asking for a human), and the disconfirmation search found that P5 gives no timing. The sensitivity test shows the pattern is not reversed when timing is required, but it then rests on one participant for each behaviour. The checks passed.
conclusions.caveat: Only some techniques state this pattern directly, and the others agree in part. It rests on one explicit quote and one quote whose timing comes from the compiler's note, and P5 gives no timing.

insights.title: The praise for the voice AI is a comparison with worse systems, not with traditional voice automation.
insights.expected: The favourable quotes would show that customers find voice AI more satisfying than the voice automation they know.
insights.found: The favourable comparators are website chat bots, a robot voice and repeating yourself, and no quote names a phone menu or interactive voice response system.
insights.why_it_matters: A favourable reaction in these interviews cannot be used as evidence that voice AI beats the voice automation it would replace.
insights.label: medium
insights.reason: This rests on the conclusion that no quote compares the voice AI with traditional voice automation, which is labelled high, and the conclusion that participants are split on the voice AI, which is labelled medium, so the insight takes the lower label. The same comparators may also reflect a low baseline from earlier tools, which the quotes cannot separate from real satisfaction.
insights.caveat: The reading depends partly on a split between favourable and unfavourable views whose balance changes with the coding. The comparators may also reflect a low starting point from earlier tools, which the quotes cannot separate from real satisfaction.

insights.title: Wanting a human may be a first reaction that fades as the call goes on.
insights.expected: The third hypothesis assumes that customers either ask for a human straight away or do not.
insights.found: P4 says they would probably want to speak to someone at first, then finds it "a really good process" as it goes on, so the same participant is on both sides at different points.
insights.why_it_matters: A route to a human at the start may matter more than whether customers keep using it later.
insights.label: medium
insights.reason: This rests on the conclusion about the third hypothesis and the conclusion about the start of the call, and both are labelled medium. The fading is stated by one participant in one quote, and no technique had a second participant to compare it with.
insights.caveat: Only one participant, in one quote, describes the wish for a human fading, and the two conclusions it builds on are each only moderately supported.

insights.title: The stated reasons for hanging up are about the introduction and a refused human, not about learning it is an AI.
insights.expected: The second hypothesis assumes that the moment of learning it is an AI is what triggers a hang-up.
insights.found: P10 gives the length of the introduction and P5 makes the hang-up conditional on not getting a human, and the material does not say when the AI is disclosed.
insights.why_it_matters: The contradiction of H2 depends on counting any early exit as evidence, and a design change to the introduction could address both stated reasons.
insights.label: medium
insights.reason: This rests on the conclusion about the second hypothesis and the conclusion about reservations tied to context, and both are labelled medium. The disconfirmation search shows that the AI itself cannot be ruled out as a driver for P5 and P10.
insights.caveat: A check found that the AI itself cannot be ruled out as a reason for the hang-ups of P5 and P10, and the material does not say when the AI is disclosed.

insights.title: The split is within people as well as between them.
insights.expected: The favourable and unfavourable quotes would come from two kinds of customer, enthusiasts and sceptics.
insights.found: P1 is favourable in one quote and annoyed in another, and P4 moves from reluctance to approval within one quote, so the quotes attach to features and moments more than to types of customer.
insights.why_it_matters: Sorting participants into accepting and rejecting groups would misrepresent these interviews.
insights.label: medium
insights.reason: This rests on the conclusion that participants are split and the conclusion about reservations tied to context, and both are labelled medium. The pattern rests on two participants, and the favourable and unfavourable groups may differ in the question each was answering and not in feeling.
insights.caveat: The pattern rests on two participants only, and the favourable and unfavourable quotes may differ because each answered a different question, not because feelings changed.

not_covered: The analysis did not show how common any of these views are among customers, because ten selected quotes from six participants cannot give a rate.
The analysis did not answer whether the first hypothesis holds, because no quote compares the voice AI with traditional voice automation.
The analysis did not observe any actual hang-up or request for a human, because every such statement is hypothetical.
Two of the eight participants, P8 and P9, have no quote, and the basis for choosing the quotes is not given, so their views were not examined.
The material does not say where in the call the AI is disclosed, so the analysis could not separate the effect of learning it is an AI from the effect of the voice, the introduction and the setting.
The process looked only at the interview material provided and did not search for outside sources, such as research on voice AI satisfaction or hang-up rates.
The process did not check the quotes against the full transcripts or recordings, which were not provided.
The process did not have a person review the results.
basis: Material given: one source, eight customer interviews on voice AI customer support, text, 512 words, with ten quotes from six of the eight participants, and three hypotheses (H1 to H3).

Techniques that ran, each as a separate agent: hypothesis tree, preprocessing sensitivity testing, case matrix, reflexive thematic analysis, framework analysis, content analysis, stance detection and analysis of competing hypotheses, each working on the request and the material.
Techniques that worked on the findings of the analysis: disconfirmation search and sensitivity analysis, each as a separate agent.
The quotation check was done by code on the findings.
Files that could not be read: none.
Quotation check by code: 146 quoted spans checked and 6 not found in the source, all six being labels or terms in quotation marks and not quotations.
Spot check by code: 55 pairs of quote and participant checked and 0 wrong, with 0 to 3 pairs checked for four of the techniques.
Repeat runs: content analysis coded the same on 4 of 4 repeats, and stance detection gave the same label on 28 of 30 targets.
Checks not done: checks that need a person were left out because the stakes are decision-informing.
Review by a person: none of the results was reviewed by a person.
The user confirmed the request after the first group of techniques by keeping it as it was.
The user chose the agreement table followed by a narrative summary as the method for combining the results.
